The enterprise AI gap is no longer anecdotal. Two independent studies just quantified it.

PwC reports that 74% of AI's economic gains are flowing to 20% of organizations. Deloitte's survey of 3,235 executives confirms the same pattern from a different angle: only 34% of companies are genuinely reimagining their business with AI, while 37% are still layering it on top of existing workflows with no meaningful structural change.

Two different methodologies. Same conclusion. The enterprise AI market is bifurcating into a small group building compounding advantage and a large group capturing efficiency gains that will commoditize as tools become universally available.

The executive implication is stark. Surface-level AI adoption — chatbots, summarization, basic automation — will not be a differentiator by 2027. Every competitor will have access to the same tools at roughly the same cost. The 20% pulling ahead are restructuring decision-making, workflows, and business models around AI capabilities. They are not adding AI to what they do. They are changing what they do.

This is not a technology gap. It is a leadership gap. The organizations in the top quintile have executive teams that treat AI as a business architecture decision, not an IT deployment.
